title: The light when every light goes out
hookLine: a king asks a sage what light a person sees by when the sun, moon and fire are all gone
carry: the self is its own light
tomorrow: who asked for sleep instead of a boon?

lines: WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON SEE BY?
AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?
cards: A king named Janaka puts a question to the sage Yajnavalkya. What light does a person see by? The sun, says the sage.
By its light we sit, go out, work, and come home. And when the sun has set? The moon.
And when the moon has set? Fire. And when the fire goes out?
Then speech: in the dark, we move toward a voice. And when speech, too, falls silent? The king keeps pushing, the way a child keeps asking why.

teach.h: THEN THE SELF IS HIS LIGHT.
teach.b: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, chapter four, and Yajnavalkya's answer, in paraphrase, is this: then the Self is his light. By that light he sits, goes out, works and comes home.
This is one of the Upanishads' great teachings about the atman: the Self isn't lit by anything.

teach.h: THE ATMAN IS THE LIGHT EVERYTHING IS SEEN BY.
teach.b: It is the light everything else is seen by. Then the sage follows the person into sleep. In dreams, he says, there are no chariots, no harnesses, no roads, but the dreamer makes chariots and harnesses and roads.
There are no joys or ponds or rivers, and the dreamer makes those too.

teach.h: IN DREAMS, THE PERSON IS HIS OWN LIGHT.
teach.b: In dream, the text says, the person becomes his own light. Nothing outside lights the scene; it's lit from within. Then comes the image this whole yoga nidra stretch could rest on.
A falcon, or any swift bird, has been flying around in the open sky. It grows tired.

teach.h: THE TIRED FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.
teach.b: It folds its wings and is carried down to its nest. In the same way, the sage says, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, there's no more wanting and no more dreaming. Deep sleep, here, isn't collapse.
It's a homecoming. So when a teacher of yoga nidra asks a room to stop doing and let the body grow heavy, they're inviting something this Upanishad already pictured.

teach.h: THE SELF IS ITS OWN LIGHT.
teach.b: What the practice adds is staying aware as it happens: the falcon lands, and the light that is the Self watches it land.

how: Hindus who study the Upanishads read Janaka's questions to Yajnavalkya on the light of the Self and on dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as resting deeply while staying aware.

o: falling asleep in class while trying to meditate
a dream so vivid you think you're awake
the sleep of yoga: resting deep while staying aware

games.q: Janaka and Yajnavalkya — tap the pairs.
p: when all of them are gone
folds its wings, goes to its nest

s: in this Upanishad, dreams are lit by the outside world
Yajnavalkya says that in dream the person becomes his own light; there are no chariots or roads, and the dreamer makes them.
the falcon image pictures deep sleep as a homecoming
the tired bird folds its wings and goes to its nest; the person hurries to where there's no wanting and no dream.
Yajnavalkya's last light, when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone, is darkness
his answer is that then the Self is the person's light.

games.q: you're Yajnavalkya. the king asks: when sun, moon, fire and speech are all gone, what light does a person see by?
o: none. then there is only dark.
games.why: Yajnavalkya says the Self is the person's light, and then follows that light into dream and deep sleep.

practice: Lie down, or let the chair take your weight, and let the day so far be a long flight: all the reaching, answering, carrying.
On one out-breath let the shoulders fall, as if folding wings; on the next, let the hands go slack; on the next, the jaw. Each out-breath, a little more landing, and stay aware of it happening.

wordCard.voice: Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Today, the Self that lights even our dreams, and the falcon folding its wings to go home.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svapna, dream. In this Upanishad, the dreamer is his own light.

carryVoice: Your line: the Self is its own light. When every other light goes out, that one is still seeing. Back tomorrow, same hill.
